title: Demonstratives
description: Point to things near and far with this, that, these, and those.

blocks.caption: Summary
blocks.html: זֶה (this, masculine), זֹאת (this, feminine), and אֵלֶּה (these) point to something near; הוּא, הִיא (that) and הֵם, הֵן (those) point to something farther away. After a noun they behave like adjectives and take the article when the noun has it: הָאִישׁ הַזֶּה (this man), הַיּוֹם הַהוּא (that day). Before a noun, without the article, they make a sentence: זֶה הָאִישׁ (this is the man).

blocks.caption: Demonstratives
blocks.html: זֶה and זֹאת agree with their noun in gender, אֵלֶּה in number. Because the demonstrative is definite by nature, a definite noun takes a definite demonstrative: הָאִישׁ הַזֶּה (this man), הָאִשָּׁה הַזֹּאת (this woman). They can also stand alone: זֶה טוֹב, "this is good".

blocks.caption: Common confusion
blocks.html: Watch the article. הָאִישׁ הַזֶּה is "this man", a phrase; זֶה הָאִישׁ is "this is the man", a sentence. And הוּא can be "he" or "that": with the article after a definite noun, as in הַיּוֹם הַהוּא, it is "that".
